utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, and good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Today is Tuesday, 5th of February, 2008. Good afternoon to all the OTP representatives, to Mr. Seselj and to all the people assisting us in our work. Before moving to some specific items, I'd like the Prosecution to introduce themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Representing the Prosecution today is Daryl Mundis, myself; and Lisa Biersay, our trial attorney; and Jasmina Bosnjakovic, our case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Welcome to this courtroom. Mr. Mundis, we are very familiar with you. I've known you since you were an attorney in many cases, and I believe my colleagues also have to deal with you in the Delic case, so welcome. I have several items to deal with before the witness is brought in. First of all, Mr. Seselj, we were informed that three of your associates and the case manager will come to the Tribunal this week. I believe your associates are going to participate in at least one of the hearings, maybe tomorrow's or the day after tomorrow. So please can you confirm this? Secondly, in case your associates come to one or two hearings, I was told that the courtroom --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, the room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- where you can have a rest during the breaks can only, besides you, contain another two people so that the four associates you have cannot be in the same room as you during breaks, since the room can contain three people. Can you confirm that your associates are going to participate in one or two of the hearings after today's?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. My legal advisors: Zoran Krasic; Aleksandar Vucic; Slavko Jerkovic; and the case manager, Marina Ragus are arriving tomorrow. The plan was that they attend on Thursday. They won't make it tomorrow because they have some business to attend to in the Registry. And I'll add they'll be able to come not more than once a month unless the issue of financing of their work is regulated. They, first and foremost, have to do the jobs, and they're living in Belgrade and only in the second place can help me. I'm surprised to hear that this room, the rest room that we can use during the break can accommodate only two persons because I remember the times of the Milosevic trial when more people could be there, plus they used the two adjacent rooms. He placed his legal advisors there and also a group of students who volunteered to assist his defence, Dutch students who volunteered and participated in preparing his defence. I saw them with my own eyes, and I was able to observe a lot during the 14 days I testified. I'm therefore surprised that I'm faced with new restrictions. The same restrictions apply in the Detention Unit. I am still unable to use the fax machine. Faxes are just handed to me at the Detention Unit. I have no confirmation and no proof that they were not copied and given to the Prosecution or somebody else before being given to me. But I'm not an eye-witness. If I were an eye-witness, I could speak about it differently. I am still short of many things in the preparation of my defence, but I am doing it successfully, as you can see, nevertheless.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to try and shed some light on this. You are telling me that Slobodan Milosevic was able to have more than two people in that room, and you fail to understand why this is being imposed on you. I'm going to check that, but I can't give you an answer straight away. At first sight, if this could be done before, there's no reason why you couldn't enjoy those facilities. With regard to your associates, they will come in, they will sit in the first row, and I'll ask them to introduce themselves because I don't know them, so I'll ask them to introduce themselves in order to get to know them. You told us that they were going to come on Thursday. The second problem we have to deal with, that's the issue of the report of Theunens, an expert witness. The Prosecution planned that the witness would start testifying next week, but beforehand the Trial Chamber would like to seek some information from you. As a reminder, because this is a very complex matter, let me remind the fundamentals thereof. On the 31st of March, 2006, the Prosecution filed a confidential motion, ex parte confidential motion, containing the Theunens report in its totality as annex 1 and in its redacted version as annex 2; and this was filed with the Trial Chamber. It was disclosed. On the 2nd October, 2006, the then-Trial Chamber had ordered the report to be disclosed, and in its entirety, to the Defence. It had also ordered that the sensitive parts of the report not be disclosed to the public. But at the time, due to the litigation opposing you to the Trial Chamber with regard to an appointment of a stand-by counsel and due to the fact that you had started a hunger strike, apparently the report was not disclosed to you. Later on, on the 17th or the 18th of May, 2007 - we're not sure as to the date - the said report was disclosed to you in its redacted version, so on the 17th or the 18th of May. From that date onwards apparently you have had the report in its redacted version. On the 14th of June, 2007, the Trial Chamber issued a decision following a reconsideration of the 2 October 2006 decision. The Trial Chamber had ordered that the entire report be disclosed, at the latest 30 days before the trial began, was to be -- that is, before November 11th, 2007. The Prosecution disclosed the report on the 3rd of October, 2007, so it had been complied with. In the 14 June 2007 decision, we also said that, at the latest 14 days after the 14 June 2007 decision had been disclosed in B/C/S, the accused was to complement his oral objection formulated on the 5th of June, 2007. I remind you that you raised an objection in court on the 5th of June, so you had been required to file an answer. Apparently you didn't within the time period prescribed. And we've just received an answer which bears the date of the 3rd of January, 2008, and at first sight this answer has been filed outside the deadline. Our problem is as follows: You know that this Trial Chamber operates in total transparency, so I tell you everything you need to know. Our question now is whether your associate who worked on the reply, when he was working on it, had the complete version or the redacted one. Why do we need to know this? If he had the complete version, there's no problem. The submissions he wrote took all the elements into account, and we could, therefore, start as of next week with the testimony. However, if he only had the redacted version, it may be that some information is missing. So I suppose you know exactly, Mr. Seselj, whether your associate worked on the complete version or whether he did on the redacted one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you answer already? I have other questions, additional questions, for you later on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm also a little bit confused concerning this supplemental report and the passages that were redacted. I got updates on two occasions, the last time a few days ago. The Prosecution is probably able to tell you the exact date when I was updated on the report of Mr. Theunens. I hope I'm pronouncing this correctly. My associate who drafted the reply is not a legal advisor. He's not a lawyer. He's a military expert. It's Bozidar Delic, one of the best Serbian military experts alive. And in his study he mainly contested the theoretical part of the Prosecution expert, Mr. Theunens. As for practical circumstances, I'll deal with that in cross-examination. At any rate the response I submitted on the 3rd of January that was written by my team member, General Bozidar Delic, is my comprehensive response to the Theunens response, regardless of the fact that Mr. Delic did not have available to him the redacted passage. As for the examination of Mr. Theunens, I believe it would be a good idea to have it as soon as possible because even for you, as the Trial Chamber, the situation would be much clearer; and it's better probably to do that before we bring a large number of crime-base witnesses. Second, I was informed on Friday by the Prosecution that they are planning to examine Theunens for eight hours. I think that's good. I would also like to have eight hours. If you remember, I have already asked once for you to increase my time from four to five hours. Eight hours is an ideal solution, and I believe it should stay that way. The Prosecution were probably able to inform you what I received a week or ten days ago. I didn't expect this matter to be discussed today, and I didn't take the file with me; and I didn't refresh my memory. But they have proper electronic records, I suppose, and they would be able to tell you. At any rate, although they probably gave me the redacted passages only then, I do not require any delay of the testimony of the Prosecution expert. I believe on the contrary, it is in the interests of the Trial Chamber and even my interest to have it as soon as possible. And I'm ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, if I understood properly, General Bozidar Delic, who assisted you in preparing the submissions filed in January 2008, only had the redacted version to work on. It was indeed impossible for him to have the entire version because there were confidential elements that could not be made known to you. So you can confirm -- you did confirm that it was the redacted version, but you added that was no problem, that you could start as early as Monday. That's good news. With regard to the time you're going to have, the Prosecution had indeed asked for eight hours and you, for five. The Trial Chamber discussed this matter and is of the view that the Prosecutor could, within five hours, submit the report of expert Theunens because we have a comprehensive report, there will be documents that will be submitted to the expert witness, and five hours is more than enough to do so. The Trial Chamber therefore decided - this is in order to inform Mr. Mundis - that the Prosecution will have five hours and the accused Seselj will also have five hours. But in addition to this, we have a related problem. It is this: The Prosecution did on the 24th of December, 2007, filed a confidential motion to add 59 pieces of evidence or exhibits to the 55 ter list -- 65 ter. I was told, Mr. Seselj, that you received the translation in your own language of the Prosecution motion. The Prosecution would wish to add 59 exhibits to the 65 ter list because they intend to submit the documents to Mr. Theunens. So we're talking about 59 documents, but I suppose you have received the list all ready. The fact that you learn of this only one week before the testimony, because we are due to start his testimony next week, is that an obstacle for you, an impediment, or not? Would you be able to start with the cross-examination next week or so with the 59 documents?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I received that material last night after 1700 hours, and I had no time to look through it because I spent all last night and the morning of today preparing for the continuation of Mr. Tomic's testimony. I cannot tell you what I think of these documents. I can only strenuously condemn this manner used by the Prosecution, who had five years to prepare the evidence in their case, and only when the trial began they began producing an avalanche of exhibits. All the exhibits of the Prosecution generally suffer from one weakness: Irrelevance and an overabundance of documents that prove nothing. You have already had occasion to hear two experts and one witness. Sometimes the Prosecution provides three binders for each, but they don't use all the material inside and they don't even tender all the documents. So they seem to be intentionally burdening me with this sea of unnecessary documents. Furthermore, this latest shipment of 67 documents will not considerably impede my cross-examination of the expert Theunens, but I believe that nevertheless you should stand in the way of this practice of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is no fault of yours. Please be reassured about that. I'm not at all criticising you. This report by Theunens, the expert witness, has 689 footnotes --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Or 699, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In other words, the expert looked into hundreds of documents. Now, the 59 new documents are mentioned in the footnotes so that General Bozidar Delic was apprised of them because they were mentioned in the footnotes. As a result this doesn't harm the accused directly, but on the substance, how is it that the Seselj file, which has been in abeyance for years, with regard to it the Prosecution at the last minute realises that there were 59 documents that were not in the 65 ter list? You may not have an answer. I would understand that. But it is frustrating, isn't it, to be faced with this sort of problem. You don't have to answer because you're just new to this case, but you might have something to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Perhaps once all of the issues concerning the expert report of Mr. Theunens have been raised, perhaps later this afternoon I can consult with my trial team and even bring in the trial attorney who will be dealing with that witness who, as the Presiding Judge correctly indicates, would be in a much better position than myself in order to address these specific issues. I can assure you that he's following the transcript from his office and if there are any -- in addition to the issues already raised, any further issues either coming from Professor Seselj or from the Trial Chamber, then we will endeavour to provide a slightly more comprehensive answer, perhaps as early as later this afternoon or this evening, before we adjourn. So I respectfully ask for a little bit of time to deal with my team and with the lawyer who's assigned to that witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. All the questions regarding the report have now been put. You, therefore, have all the information you need. Let me now read in private session two very short oral rulings. Mr. Registrar, can we move to private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're now back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, you wanted to say something, to give a number, I believe? Mr. Mundis, did you want to say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Nothing further, Your Honours. The next witness will simply be led by my colleague, Ms. Biersay, when we get to that stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Ms. Biersay, you're going to finish the examination-in-chief. You still had 35 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what you're going to do. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Before beginning, Your Honour, I believe you had a question with respect to designation of exhibits. I've been advised that what has been marked as Exhibit 155 will now be remarked or recategorised as Exhibit P34, just for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Therefore, 155 becomes P34. Let's have the Witness brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may sit down. Mr. Tomic, the examination-in-chief is now going to resume. Ms. Biersay, who is with us, has 35 minutes to finish this examination-in-chief, and then Mr. Seselj will take over and start the cross-examination. I now give the floor to Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, I'd like to direct your attention to the final section of your expert report, specifically page 93. Do you have that report available to you?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, generally speaking, this section deals with the election results from approximately 1990 to 2000; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could you describe for the Court what was your primary resource for that section of your report?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I used work published by Serbian politician -- politiologists, who was a specialist who worked on political parties in Serbia and Yugoslavia and on elections.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, that is -- that book is described as -- is identified as 65 ter number 2568.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, in the course of your research into this area of elections from that time period that we just discussed, could you tell us what you learned about Mr. Seselj's participation in the 1990 presidential elections?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I said previously, at first Vojislav Seselj headed a party that was not recognised by authorities, so he is running as an independent, representing a group of citizens, according to the law at the time, and obtained about 90.000 votes, which was not much at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Approximately what percentage was that?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't really remember, but the Socialist Party obtained 2.3 million votes and the main opposition party, which was the Serbian Renewal Party, obtained more than 790.000 votes. So you see that the score of Mr. Seselj was quite low. The Chetnik Serbian Movement was at the time still a very marginal movement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question. I'm sorry to interrupt. Witness, please, could you please remind me, these were elections that he didn't have much time to prepare for; is that it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And why is it that he did not have time to prepare for those elections?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because in October 1990, when he was in the center of Belgrade to have petitions signed asking for the tomb of former President Tito to be removed, he was also trying to recruit volunteers at the time to send them to Croatia. So he was arrested with a list that had more than 100 names, and I think that he was sentenced to about 15 days in jail. But he was also sentenced in -- earlier for having organised demonstrations that had been banned by the authorities. So he had 15 days for jail when altogether he had about 90 days in jail to be enforced.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, with respect to 65 ter number 2568, could we please see the English ERN page, which is 03599-966. And, for the record, this is the page number corresponding to Vladimir Goati's book "Elections in FRY from 1990 to 1998." That page number in e-court is page 103. And if we could please zoom in on the table 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Tomic, does this reflect the information on which you relied for your report as far as the results of the presidential elections of 1990 in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is one of the books I used. This table gives the official tables that had been disclosed by the electoral committee of the country at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution would request that this be marked for identification. I would seek some guidance from the Court about whether the Court would prefer to have the entire book admitted into evidence or if you would prefer that the Prosecution select the pages that are most relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, do you have any objections to tend to admit the entire book, or not?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will deal with that book in my cross-examination a bit. This is an author who was always expressly active against the Serb Radical Party. But as for the statistical data he provides, they are correct. All the statistical information is correct. His interpretation, however, is subjective, partial, and tendentious, and I will be referring to this in my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Trial Chamber has decided to give a final number only to this table that we have on page 2 of 6 of this book. So this is what we admit, the table giving us the result of the presidential elections. Mr. Registrar, could we have a number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the table will be Exhibit P155. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, who won the December 1990 presidential elections?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Slobodan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Do you know --

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time he was head of the Serbian Socialist Party.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not after his victory in that elections, do you know whether or not Mr. Seselj sent him a letter?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall this.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could you describe for the members of the Court whether or not there were any public expression of mutual support between Milosevic and Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at the time it can't be said. Mr. Seselj was heading a party that was not recognised at the time. He had just been sentenced, convicted and sentenced, in October 1990; so at the time you can't say that there is mutual support or collaboration between the two entities, between the Serbian Socialist Party and the Chetnik Serbian Movement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please, I'm listening to you, but I was also looking at the other candidates at the time and right now there are presidential elections going on so the topic is quite interesting. Mr. Seselj is representing a citizens group and has 96.277 votes, but I also note that candidate 9 and 10, who've very little votes, 22.000 for one and 17.000 for another, are also citizens groups, also representing citizens groups. So we have three citizens groups, but what are they representing? Did they have an electoral platform? Did they have any project? What exactly is the difference between Mr. Guzic and Mr. Seselj? Between Mr. Aleksov and Mr. Guzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't really talk about these candidates, but at the time in order to run for president, if you didn't represent a recognised political party, you had to collect a certain amount of signatures in order to run. And at the time in Serbia a great number of political parties just sprung up and were created. Tens or hundreds of parties were actually created. So they were -- several political parties who ran for different elections, including the presidential elections, but they represented absolutely nothing. They had no support in society. Those were marginal candidates and represented nothing in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But according to you a candidate that has less than 2 per cent of the votes, does he represent anything or does he represent nothing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, for example, Sulejman Ugljanin, the SDA, representing the Muslims, Serbian Muslims, had about 2.18 per cent of votes and did obtain quite a number of Muslim votes. So according to the size of the community he was representing, it's a good score, but it is quite marginal nationally, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, and what about the candidate number five, Mr. Seselj? With 1.9 per cent of votes, what did he represent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, at the time what you see is that the SPS is the dominant party. Slobodan Milosevic was elected right away so the others, Mr. Seselj's party, was very marginal and didn't have a great echo in Serbian society.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Excuse me. Just for clarification, what is shown in column C and D, I believe, is that -- in column C is the deputies, number of deputies, and only in column D do we find the percentages; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, regarding the presidential election, you have the number of votes first expressed during the election, then the percentage according to the entire constituency in the country. 65 per cent of the constituency voted for -- no, 65 per cent of voters voted for Milosevic, representing only 46 per cent of the total constituency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, column D represents the total voters -- the percentage in relation to the total voters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. According to all people who voted or all people who had the right to vote?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Column C is the votes expressed, people who went to vote, and column D corresponds only to the percentage in relation to the entire constituency, 46 per cent of the entire constituency, which was quite a good score at the time for Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Moving forward to 1992, were there elections held on May 31st of 1992?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were federal elections at the end of May 1992. The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, with Serbia -- bringing together Serbia and Montenegro was actually created, and the members of the federal parliament had to be elected at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could you describe the backdrop against which that election was held?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at the time - this is the spring of 1992 - as I just said the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was set up. A constitution was set up also and drafted, but without the opposing political parties taking part to it, to this drafting. So these opposing parties boycotted the elections of May 31st, 1992. Furthermore, there was a war going on in BiH. The war started in April or May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Around that period did Milosevic call Mr. Seselj his favourite opposition politician?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were a few statements in early March 1992 where Slobodan Milosevic said that among all the opposing -- all his opponents, his favourite was Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What you're saying, was it an ideological presence or did that mean that it was a man he would challenge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe at the time there was a convergence between the two parties. Both parties defended the Serbian national ideas in Serbia as well as in BiH. So ideologically, they were very close, coming closer. And in May 1992 it seems that it was the first time that Slobodan Milosevic met with Vojislav Seselj officially, you know, and asked him officially to intensify his efforts to send volunteers to BiH, and this is May 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's an ideological convergence, this is what you answered to the Presiding Judge; but you also answered and added that it had something to do with the conflict going on. So there was also convergence regarding the means to be used in the conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in one of Vojislav Seselj's books, this meeting of May 1992 is mentioned, a meeting between the Serbian president and Mr. Seselj. Slobodan Milosevic explicitly asked for more volunteers to be sent from the Serbian Radical Party, to be sent to the BiH. Slobodan Milosevic promised all logistical support required to help send these volunteers and Vojislav Seselj mentions that this help continued -- was very effective and continued until September 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please, there's something I don't understand and maybe you can help me. According to what you're saying in your report, it seems that Slobodan Milosevic asked for Mr. Seselj's help to send volunteers. The country is in war, is at war; the country was in a situation of conflict. So why can't all soldiers be drafted? Why do you have to ask for Mr. Seselj's support? How do you explain this? Let me give you an example. During World War I, you know, in 1914, France, UK, drafted, you know, sent mobilisation orders. They didn't call on political parties to send volunteers. So why is it that Mr. Milosevic would suddenly ask for Mr. Seselj's support to send volunteers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, when the Croatian war started, during the military operations in 1991, there was a mobilisation of all reservists in Serbia and all soldiers in Serbia, and they were incorporated into the JNA at the time. But this mobilisation or this draft wasn't very positive, wasn't really welcomed. There were a lot of desertions and the population just didn't want to join, and this led to problems, recruiting problems. And so at the time the power just -- was in a difficult situation. Many just did not heed the call, if I could say so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So that would be why Slobodan Milosevic made this request to Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this could be one of the reasons. Slobodan Milosevic also had something in mind. He wanted to withdraw the JNA from BiH while leaving the infrastructure in place for the Serbian army and BiH. So the idea was to mobilise the Serbs in BiH, but we also know that there were some special troops that were sent from Serbia to Bosnia during the war.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Mr. President, I waited for the members of the Trial Chamber to complete their questions. My objection is to the manner in which the expert answered your previous question. If the expert says that Slobodan Milosevic made several statements in which he said that among the opposition leaders he liked me best - those are the words of the expert - the expert has to tell you very precisely where and when Milosevic said this. This is not just an ordinary witness who heard something somewhere. It's a witness who studied things. He must have evidence for what he says. You should insist that he provide it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. On this specific item, when did Slobodan Milosevic was his favourite opponent -- when did he say that and where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe it was in early March 1992 during a meeting with officers of the Yugoslav Army. I was in Belgrade at the time and I read that in the paper, "Borba" or in the "Vreme" magazine. It's well known. Anyone interested in political life in Serbia knows this. And I know that Robert Thomas, which is a British researcher on the political life in Serbia in the 1990s, reaffirms that this was actually said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said that you yourself were in Belgrade in 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, at the time I was in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You may resume.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, with respect to 65 ter number 2568, may we now see e-court page 104, please, specifically table 5. For the record, the heading reads: "Votes and Mandates Won in Chamber of Citizens of Federal Assembly of FRY." And may that page also be marked for identification, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour that will be MFI P156.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, looking at table 5, could you quickly summarize the outcome in the number of votes between the SRS and the SPS?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You note that the Serbian Radical Party obtains a great number of votes of the first -- compared to December 1990. 96.000 in the first one and now more than a million, so there was a jump ahead of the Radical Serbian Party. But there's an erosion of the socialist party. Earlier the other one had 200, 300.000 voters and now there's only 1.600.000 some left. So the SRS seem to have attracted a good number of voters from the SPS at the time. And DZVM, which is the party representing the Hungarian minority, obtained a very little amount of votes, but quite important in relation to the Hungarian community living in Serbia. But you see that most opposition parties at the time boycotted this vote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm interested in these results of 1992. I note that there were -- there's 12 per cent of the ballots that are deemed to be invalid. Is there a reason for this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, maybe rather than boycotting, some people just said that they oppose the election by just scratching the bulletins. I don't know what they did.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm sorry if my continued interruptions bother you, but you should not permit this evident falsification of statistical data. The number of votes from presidential elections in December 1990 cannot be measured against those of the parliamentary elections in May 1992. The expert should have offered you the number of votes at the parliamentary elections in 1990 in order to compare them with the parliamentary elections in May, because in 1990 Slobodan Milosevic received many more votes than his party did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. In terms of elections, this table is not a table that compares one election to another. This table deals with one single election, election to the Federal Assembly of FRY. He see that there's a proportional system with a majority rule and this is why you aggregate the number of deputies. SPS has 57 and the others have 30 -- 43 and 30. So this is not a presidential election. Does this change anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have no element to compare anything because the Chetnik Serbian did not run for the 1990 elections, so it would be more logical to compare one presidential election to another presidential election. But was the only order of magnitude I had. This was the two only tables I could compare. Of course, during a presidential election a candidate coming from a party may obtain a great more votes than the party would for a federal election, a parliamentary election.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the fact that the SPS here obtained 1.665.000 votes, does this prove that Slobodan Milosevic was eroding and that the SRS was actually booming or climbing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Slobodan Milosevic will run for presidential election later on in December 1992 and there will be less of an erosion than we have here in this table. But if you add the number of votes for both parties, you have the two parties that are champions of the Serbian national -- of Serbian nationalism.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Seselj, you'll have the cross-examination to go back to all these topics, unless what you have to say is essential now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it is of vital importance. The Prosecution could easily give you the outcome of the parliamentary elections of 1990 so you can see the total number of votes of the Socialist Party, and then in that light look at the statement of this witness that the electorate of the Socialist Party became scattered. The socialists had 1.664.485 votes in May 1992, and then the Prosecution can tell you how many votes they had in December 1990, and then you will be able to decide for themselves whether the electorate of the Socialist Party was lost, whether the Radical Party got their votes, or maybe some other party profited from that as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We took good note of what you said. Indeed, when you compare elections, it is better to compare presidential elections or legislative elections.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand. I do agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you agree. The witness is in agreement with you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: At the end of this previous sentence by the accused was "or maybe the radicals won over the votes of some other parties."

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Also in e-court page 104, Mr. Registrar, if we could focus on table 6. And also in the same 65 ter Exhibit 2568 if we could also show Mr. Tomic e-court page 105 as well. And we would request that this be marked for identification as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe a final number. No need to have it marked for identification. There's no challenge to this. We're going to have final numbers. Please, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, table number 5 will be Prosecution Exhibit P156; table number 6 will be Prosecution Exhibit P157; and table number 8 will be Prosecution Exhibit P158.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And just to expedite things, we will also move for the admission of e-court page 106 as well, tables 9 and 10.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Table 9 will be Exhibit P159 and table 10 Exhibit P160.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, if you could focus your attention on table 6, which is P157, could you summarize the results encapsulated in that table?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There, again, these are elections to the Federal Assembly and the opposition parties participated in these elections.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: In what year?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In December 1992. The first elections were in May so these were a few months later. And we can see that the Socialist Party of Serbia and the Radical Party get less votes, less votes than a few months earlier, but there is a greater participation of other political parties. So the array of parties is greater. No major changes between the two main parties coming to the first positions ahead of the other parties compared to the May elections.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And now I'll direct your attention to P159, which is table --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. Witness, before we move to this exhibit, I was looking at the number of voters, close to 7 million, and we see "turn-out" in English or that's the participation rate. We have a rate of 67.4 per cent, so there was quite a major participation turn-out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, at the time because the opposition parties were participating, which was not the case in 1990. We have a larger turn-out here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because there was a presidential election last Sunday and the turn-out was over 60 per cent, I think it was 61 per cent. And here we have 67 per cent. So was it a record rate, a record turn-out at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's quite a strong turn-out, but with regard to the Serbian presidential elections, there were several elections in Serbia after the year 2000 where the rate was under -- the turn-out rate was under 50 per cent, and you could not be elected if you had above -- not above 50 per cent. The law was changed. You can now be elected president of Serbia if there are under 50 per cent. That's why they insisted on the turn-out rate when there are presidential elections. For many years they failed in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Directing your attention to table 9, which is P159.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: If we could have that for Mr. Tomic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nine.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I believe that's 11. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could you describe for us what, if any, impact the SRS had in the victory of the -- of Milosevic in conjunction with the SPS in those elections of 1992, December?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We realised here that the Serbian Radical Party did not run any candidate to the presidential election in December 1992 in Serbia. It called for support to Milosevic at the time because the latter appeared to champion the same national orientation as the Serbian Radical Party. So basically you have an opposition between two candidates; on the one hand Milosevic heading the SPS, he was the then president of Serbia; and Milan Panic, who was the head of the federal government prior to these elections.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And now, Mr. Registrar, if we could go to P160, which is table 10. For the record votes, the title is: "Votes and Mandates Won in National Assembly of Serbia (December 13th 1993)."

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, could you describe for the Court what happened in late 1993 with respect to the no-confidence vote.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the parliament elections of 1992 in Serbia, the Socialist Party did not have the majority in the National Assembly. It then formed a minority government that was supported, depending on the questions they dealt with, by the -- in parliament by the SRS. So confidence to the government was withdrawn by the SRS, but there was no such vote as such in the assembly because Milosevic decided to dissolve the assembly in autumn 1993. Therefore, at the time there was lack of understanding between the -- fallout between the SPS and the SRS with regard to the events of the Vance-Owen Plan. That's when difference started to appear, when the plan was proposed in spring 1993. And at the time of autumn 1993, you have a major opposition between the two political formations and a campaign is initiated by the Socialist Party in Serbia against the SRS. It was a major media campaign and the SRS saw a drop of half the votes it had gained during these elections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In a word you mentioned the Vance-Owen Plan. Could you tell us why or how the SRS was in favour of the plan and the SPS was against it? Was that the political stake?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In spring 1993, Slobodan Milosevic organised -- took a new turn to his policy. He agreed with the peace plan as proposed by Vance and Owen. He was of the view that the FRY and Serbia were under economic embargo since June 1992 and that after all the Serbian national interests were more or less satisfied in Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. But this position was not adopted by other parties, including the SRS, and some say that as of spring 1993 Milosevic moved from a so-called nationalist policy to a more pacifist and had more support from the major powers.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could now have 65 ter number 1764, please. And, for the record, that's the Vance-Owen Peace Plan dated 2 January 1993. And we'd seek the admission of that map.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit number P161.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'm now showing you, Mr. Tomic, P161. Mr. Tomic, is this the Vance-Owen Peace Plan that you just discussed with the Bench?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, it is the peace plan that was going to divide Bosnia into ten regions.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could inquire how many minutes I have left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are we going to know straight away? I mean time applies, doesn't it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have used 3 hours and 45 minutes. You have another 15 minutes left, 1-5.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And just for planning purposes, when will be take the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we could have the break now. Fine. Let's have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You have 15 minutes left. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, have you heard of the phrase "Red Vojvoda" or "Bloody Vojvoda"?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Red Vojvoda", yes, but not the "Bloody Vojvoda."

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And in what context have you heard the "Red Vojvoda"?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's when Vojislav Seselj started being seen as a true ally of the -- of Milosevic's party, when the radicals supported the power in Serbia. This was when this phrase was coined and circulated among political leaders in the opposing parties mainly. But not just in the opposing parties. Also in people who were faithful to the Ravna Gora Movement.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could now see 65 ter number 1811, please. For the record, that's the "Programme Orientation of the Serbian Radical Party of the Republika Srpska published in Western Serbia, number 2, July 1993."

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, could you describe what we're looking at? What is the "Programme of the Serbian Radical Party of Republika Srpska"?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well this is the platform of the Serbian Radical Party of Republika Srpska, which was one of the branches of the Serbian Radical Party. This programme dates back to 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if you could indeed enlarge paragraph 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, could you --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Before we do that, could I have this marked as identification, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be MFI P162.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, could you read paragraph 1, please.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The Serbian Radical Party proposes as its primary objective complete national, spiritual, cultural, economic and political unity of the Serbian people. The Republika Srpska and the Serbian Radical Party will strive to establish a free, independent and, above all, democratic Serbian state comprising all of Serbian lands on the territory of the former Yugoslavia."

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And now to draw your attention, if we could go to page 2 of the B/C/S version, Mr. Registrar, to paragraph 5. Mr. Tomic, could you now please read paragraph 5 for us?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The RS SRS believes that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia should be supported as an intermediate solution which could ensure that requesting international recognition of sovereignty be avoided, and with that, the calculated conditioning and blackmailing by other foreign countries. We consider that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia as one of the options for speeding up the process of uniting Serbs and Serbian lands into one common Serbian state by retaining the international and legal continuity of the Yugoslav state."

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And could you explain to us how the political objectives stated in this programme compares with the one stated in the programme for the SRS in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The objectives are the same but the formulation is different. In item 1 where there's a unification principle for all Serbian land, there is no mention of all the territories that should be incorporated into this single Serbia, whereas in the SRS platform we have all the regions that are detailed and that are mentioned and all the regions that should be included in this Serbian state. And here there -- actually, the political reality is taken into account, the reality of the moment, of what was happening at the time in 1993. The Chetnik Movement was not really attached to a united Yugoslavia, but they had to accept the FRY as long as the Serbian Republic of Krajina in Croatia or the Republika Srpska be attached to this state. And there were a few statements going in that direction, actually, from all state entities set up in Croatia and in BiH, but Serbia never gave a positive answer to these statements. So the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia seemed to be the vehicle that could be used to recognise a state, bringing together all Serbs, given it was very difficult to have recognition as a single state, as an independent state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have three questions. First, you've just read us paragraph 5 of a text. Could you tell us what is the date of this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1993, but I don't remember the month.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. 1993. At the time BiH had been recognised as an independent state.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At paragraph 5, on the last sentence it is said, "continuity of the Yugoslav state." It seems that it's their project, so it seems that they want a Serbian territory which would be the continuity of the Yugoslav state. Is this how this sentence should be interpreted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the FRY believed that it was the continuity of the former Yugoslav state. Of course there were some republics that had separated from it. But for the Serbian Radical Party this was a way, a legal vehicle, a legal way, to have recognition of a state that would bring together all, what they called, Serbian lands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So according to you this paragraph should be interpreted or construed as such. The ones who drafted this wanted a legal recognition of a Serbian state.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A Serbian state, yes, but that would be provisionally called Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. This was one of the possibilities that was envisaged, one of the possible scenarios.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this seems to be one of the options. And what are the other options?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there were a few options that were looked into for, number 1, unifying the republic -- Serbian Republic of Krajina and the Republika Srpska, so unifying the western Serbian countries in the first step, in so-called western Serbia, for example, and then in the second step they would be unification between that western Serbian state with Serbia per se or a Serbia Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And this in a democratic and legal way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this was -- all these states were set up during war, the Republic of Krajina and Republika Srpska. But at the time there had been a number of proclamations of independence but in Belgrade the authorities did not approve this. It seemed that this embarrassed them more than anything, this bothered them more than anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You've just added something very important. This option to have unification of Krajina and Republika Srpska didn't really please Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, nothing -- no positive answer was given to this. For example, the Serbian Republic of Krajina said that it was part of Serbia and that it would apply the laws of Serbia on its territory and that it would be de facto attached to Serbia and it would detach itself from Croatia, but Serbia did not heed that call, positively anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you're talking about Serbia, who are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What about Slobodan Milosevic? What was his point of view? Yes, if you could please speak slower.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The objective was to set up a single Serbian state, but this raised practical problems, because if you had enlarged Serbian states, there was a problem with international recognition. So caution had to be exerted and caution was exerted from Belgrade regarding this. But the policy of the support of the Serbs was towards the creation of a single Serbian state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But at the time there was the Vance-Owen Plan that was going on, wasn't it? Was all this compatible with the Vance-Owen Plan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Vance-Owen Plan created a problem to the partisans of the Serbian national cause because there was no territorial continuity between the different regions that would be set up within Bosnia-Herzegovina. The main problem was the corridor, the Brcko corridor in the north of Bosnia, because there, there was discontinuity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have the map on the screen, the Vance-Owen map.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And that was P161, or 65 ter number 1764.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We have it on screen and we see -- could you tell us where this corridor would be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This corresponds to region number 3 in the very north of the country. Here there was a strategic access that was absolutely essential for the Serbian leaders of the time, and it was totally inconceivable for the political parties supporting Republika Srpska to recognise the Vance-Owen Plan, because here you've got Bosanska Krajina that would have been completely isolated and that would not be connected to Serbia through this corridor. And this was a main challenge. This was at stake during combat in 1991 and 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 4 to 3, is that it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Number 4 would have to be linked to region number 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And there it was not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely, it was not. It was separated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And this is one of the reasons why there was opposition from Serbs in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Some in Serbia and also in the Serbian Republic of BiH because the Serbs of Bosnia-Herzegovina did not want this peace plan and rejected the peace plan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Ms. Biersay, I'm sorry I interrupted your questions, but I wanted to understand what was at stake here, and I wanted to take advantage of the presence of the witness. So you may resume.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Leaving the events of 1993, if I could ask Mr. Registrar to bring up 65 ter number 264. For the record, that's described as "Seselj's Interview with Pogledi, Published in One Politics as a Challenge to the Conscience" and specifically this exhibit includes pages 66 to 72.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, do you recognise that exhibit?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is one of the books I studied, indeed, and I quoted on several occasions of my report.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Specifically it's in footnote 183 on page 88 of your report; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which footnote is it, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I believe it is footnote 183. Forgive me, 193.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is not the right footnote in my document.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: But do you recognise this document as being one on which your report was based?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. I took quite a few good quotations from this piece of work.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, we'd seek the admission of 65 ter number 264.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit number P163.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: In this interview does Mr. Seselj discuss the presence of the SRS in Croatia and BiH?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he does.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And could you summarize for us what that presence was in BiH?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the document in every detail. I don't remember its contents. But he does allude to his trips through Bosnia, Krajina, Slavonia, but these themes are recurrent ones in each of his works. So I did not memorise each of the interviews.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do we have the date of this interview?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: The date, Your Honour, I believe, is 31st of May, 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And it's found on the last page of the exhibit. If I could ask Mr. Registrar to go to page 3 in the -- in e-court, in the B/C/S, for Mr. Tomic, and similarly page 3 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Directing your attention to the page that's before us, on that page it does describe Mr. Seselj's involvement in Bosnia, the Krajina, Slavonia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, he's being asked about his trip going to Bosnia-Herzegovina because in a previous document we had seen that he had set up a command, a Chetnik command, in the area of Romanija and here, which he was supposed to take part in a broadcast in Sarajevo, there was a protest that was organised in Sarajevo against the said broadcast to which he was invited.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further question for Mr. Tomic. With respect to what has been marked as MFI P162, which is 65 ter number 1811, I would move for its admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will become Exhibit number P162.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And before I sit down, Your Honour, just to make the cross-examination perhaps a bit more smooth, we would request any documents that Mr. Seselj intends to show the witness that is not readily available on the e-court system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Ms. Biersay. Mr. Seselj, the Prosecution are asking whether you have documents that you seek to submit to the witness in your cross-examination? If you have some, please tell us what they're about.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I do have several documents, some of which I will show because it's important for them to be seen visually by the witness, whereas I will provide some others tomorrow, asking for them to be copied for the Prosecution. I received a certain number of documents today by fax. It's up to me to offer them and it's up to you to accept them or not. I don't have the same resources at my disposal that the Prosecution has and as you have seen, in spite of all their resources, they give themselves a lot of leeway in the presentation of documents. I will therefore begin my cross-examination and it's for you to intervene if something is not correct in my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tomic, in what year were you born?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Novi Sad, in Vojvodina, in the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What is your father by ethnicity or nationality?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What is your religion?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You're an atheist, then? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not christened. It doesn't mean that I'm an atheist. This is the way I've lived so far, and it's fine by me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I don't object. It's up to you. But I have to know everything about you and these are things that I have not been ascertain in any other way. I hope you don't mind. What university did you graduate from?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I studied in the National Institute of Oriental Languages and Civilisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Paris. It is "Ecole Superiore."

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What is the precise title of your university diploma?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Diplome d'Etudes Appliquees, third cycle studies in France. Usually called DEA in French, advanced study diploma or degree.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, let's be very precise?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As soon as you graduated, did you acquire the title of master of arts or did you have to go to a post-graduate course, take exams, defend an MA thesis? That's what I would like to know.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to get this degree I've just mentioned I had to write a dissertation of some hundred pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I think you're avoiding answering my question. How long is the regular course of studies?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you do not answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The problem is that it's difficult for me to hear, to understand, because Mr. Seselj speaks very loudly and I hear both French and what he says, so I'm a bit confused in my earphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] DEA is a third cycle degree. Before the third cycle there's a first and a second cycle.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So did you get a masters degree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that same institute and in order to get this masters degree I wrote a dissertation of some hundred pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this advanced study degree, is that prior to a Ph.D.?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So after DEA you have a third cycle Ph.D.?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you start research. You may complete it or not as part of your Ph.D. studies.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It seems I'm the only one who doesn't understand anything here. This diploma of yours, does it correspond to a four-year course of studies in Belgrade at the university? Is that the maitrise diploma?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at the institute where I studied, the first cycle was three years instead of two years in other French universities. Thereafter, you would have two years that would correspond to licence and masters degree. So that DEA, that advanced study degree, was after -- at the end of this sixth year of study. That means that the programme, the curriculum, is somewhat different at that institute compared to curricula in other French universities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well. It's clearer to me now. When you completed those three years, the first cycle, what was your title then?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we don't have a title as such. You just have a degree, a first-cycle degree. I'm not aware of any title in France for that level of studies.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'll rephrase my question to make it simpler. When you obtained the first cycle diploma, you finished this three-year course of studies, what job are you qualified to perform? Can you teach languages in primary or secondary school? Can you be a translator somewhere? What job are you qualified for after those first three years of study?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear everything, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I hope, as I have to repeat the question, it will be deducted from my time. When you completed this first course of three-year studies you became qualified to perform a job. What specific job did you become qualified to perform after completing the three-year course of studies? To teach languages in a school, to be a journalist, to be a translator?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After three years of study you get a degree, but it's not enough. You need to have at least an additional year of study in order to apply for a specific exams, admission exams or tests, to become a teacher, for instance, or something equivalent.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Does this mean that with the first cycle of three years, you have no professional qualification?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Some degree of knowledge is acknowledged. That's precisely the purpose of this degree, to validate the knowledge you have acquired. And then later, depending on your field of interest, based on that degree you can find a job. That's already enough in and of itself, but later on it depends on the positions. If you want to become a teacher, that's something -- part of public, you're a civil servant, so you have to meet specific criteria to be entitled to apply. And say if you want to be a cadre, a higher position, you must have at least what is called a licence in France.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You still haven't explained anything to me, but what I understand is after the first three years of studies you are not able to perform any kind of job, and had you not undertaken the second cycle, you would not have a profession.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. When you study there where you studied at this Institute of Oriental Languages and Civilisation, you're not planning to get a job after three years only. My idea was to have -- to study in the long term. I was not thinking of getting a job. I was still a student then.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well. We've lost a lot of time. You're avoiding answering my question. You studied languages --

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that we have different university study systems, you see.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that, but you're avoiding answering my question. Well, then, you undertook this second two-year course of study and received a title of master of arts?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I would object to the characterisation of the witness' testimony. He has, in fact, answered the question, and Mr. Seselj continues to ask him the same question despite his answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I'm going to intervene because apparently Mr. Seselj does not understand how studying is carried out in that institute. Its purpose is the teaching of oriental or eastern languages.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And also if you decide, civilisation, history, and geography.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And when you graduate, what do you become? Is it to become an interpreter, a teacher, a journalist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are all sorts of profiles depending on your interest. I can't generalise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you, what was your profile? What kind of job did you want?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was interested in history. I wanted to teach at university initially.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The history of Balkans?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the history of the Balkans.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Please proceed, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So this second degree, the maitrise diploma you acquired, corresponds to the title of master of arts; is that right?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What corresponds to the masters degree is the fifth year of study. I mean, there's -- the first cycle is three years long and corresponds to the licence is four years, and the masters is five years. The final diploma for post-graduate corresponds to the sixth year of study. So I specialised in history as of the fifth year of my studies, corresponding to the masters degree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But your dissertation, your masters dissertation, was on which topic and your DEA dissertation was which?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I studied the student's movement in Yugoslavia between 1968 and 1971. It was the same topic for the two dissertations, but the DEA study was just the continuation of the work that I had already started for my masters thesis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough as to tell me the precise title of that research, not the -- what it's about but the topic of your dissertation?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The student movement in Yugoslavia between 1968 and 1971 and the authoritarian turn of the Yugoslav regime in 1972," I think that was more or less the way it was called.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So it's a topic from modern history. From your bibliography, I see that you never dealt with ancient Serb history or older Serbian history.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read books on later history, but the history of Middle Ages is either specialisation which requires knowing a certain number of languages and you can't be -- you can't just work on the Middle Ages and at the same time also work on modern history. You can't do both.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, I know what you can and can't do, but I want to establish what you did and what you did not do. When you say that you read books from older history, it's like me telling you that I read all the works by Balzac, Emile Zola, Viktor Goh [phoen] and Standal. So who has read what doesn't mean anything, but you don't have a single reference showing that you're an expert for older Serbian history.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I followed classes on the Middle Ages and on the following period, on the Ottoman Empire. However, my research was not on this period. I believe that to do that it would be best to know ancient Greek, ancient Latin, in order to be able to study all possible sources available for that period of time. I believe that there were a number of competencies that were required that I did not have, and I decided not to specialise on the Middle Ages. As a rule historians tend to specialise themselves from a given period. You hardly ever have a historian that will cover an entire period, all eras. Historians always specialised in one period, one century, a couple centuries, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: As an alleged specialist or expert for recent history and modern history, you were recruited to write an expert report on the ideology of Serbia in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. That's what matters to me. And we see from your references that you are not an expert on that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From two years, from 1999 to 2001, I taught on southern Slavs --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not catch the period.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I also taught on the Yugoslav period at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please repeat the period of time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Between 1999 and 2001 I lectured at University Paris for the Sabon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you were lecturing what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The history of Yugoslav countries in the nineteenth century.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, if I, for example, were a professor at a French university and had a Ph.D., and if I was being tried in France before a French court because of my ideology and its practical repercussions, would a single French court, in your opinion, ask you with the status of master of arts to be an expert witness to evaluate the ideology of a person with a Ph.D. who is a full-time university professor?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
