utterances.text: I don't know what criteria they use in the French legal systems to call on experts. Their expertise are required in several areas, psychology, and so on; I don't know what criteria are used. I don't know the French legal system, at least in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But you are aware of elementary logic and some academic ways. You said that as of 1999 you are an associate, you cooperate with the French Ministry of Defence for strategic issues.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I drafted some research for the French ministry of -- French Ministry of Defence, notably for the Strategic Institute.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Wait before the interpretation is finished.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wrote three reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What month in 1999?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in 1999. I remember that, but I can't tell you the month exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Unlike you, Mr. Tomic, I remember everything I did 30 years ago when I was a young assistant. But well, you don't remember.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was not essential for me --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I object.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It doesn't matter for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What Mr. Seselj remembers or doesn't remember is not pertinent for the questions posed to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, absolutely. What's important is what the witness knows or what the witness does not know, what the witness recalls and what the witness does not recall. Please continue, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This question is very important to me because I'm challenging the credibility of this expert witness. To the best of my knowledge he worked for the French Ministry of Defence when there were airstrikes against Serbia and the FRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is that correct, Mr. Tomic?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is work that I did afterwards. I was not employed by the Ministry of Defence as a salaried worker. I was just part of a project. And for these projects, there are tenders that are launched and then the different -- there's call for tenders and then I tendered to see if I could get my research paper done, and it was the international protectorate in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time. It was not dealing with the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you said that you made three study papers for the Ministry of Defence. Could you tell us exactly what topics they were on? You just told us one, could you give us the two others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The second one was on the national Serbian question after the fall of Slobodan Milosevic and the outlook. Secondly -- thirdly, the democratic transition in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia after 2000, and the research question here was the security aspects.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what was the purpose of these research papers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the Ministry of Defence has teams that follow what's going on in the Balkans, notably in the former Yugoslavia. They collect information through the ordinary channels, through embassies, through their representatives in the area also, and they also call on outside people to make research in order to cross the -- these different analyses, in order to have a debate between all the people working in the ministry and the researchers that are outside the ministry and specialised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, at that time the French defence ministry was headed by a socialist, Alain Richard.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Alain Richard is a self-declared Atlantist and very committed to close cooperation with the USA; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer positively. I never really wondered about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Alain Richard is a close associate of Michel Rocard; right?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that Michel Rocard is one of four French representatives of the otherwise Anglo-Saxon International Crisis Group?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe. I do not know the exact makeup of this organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Are you aware that the International Crisis Group was set up by Morton Abramowitz, former US ambassador to Ankara and otherwise the main arms supplier to Afghanistani Mujahedins at the time of the Mujahedin insurgency against the Soviet army in Afghanistan? Just say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You don't know. I won't insist, then. Do you know that Morton Abramowitz was a special advisor to the separatist terrorist Albanian delegation, to the Rambouillet negotiations, where Serbs were faced with an ultimatum?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possible but I don't know this exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that the remaining three French members of the International Crisis Group Simone Weill, Jacques Delors and Christine Ockrent?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about the fact that Christine Ockrent belonged to this organisation, but for the two others, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The names are not on the transcript. Could you please repeat the names, Mr. Seselj. The names are not on the transcript yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Simone Weill, Jacques Delors and Christine Ockrent.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Christine Ockrent is the wife of Bernard Kouchner, the current foreign minister of France.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Bernard Kouchner is the leader of a fierce anti-Serb campaign going on in France for the past 17 years; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not give an opinion on this. This is your appreciation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But you are an expert, Mr. Tomic. You should have an opinion on that as well. But never mind.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bernard Kouchner is the minister of foreign affairs and as a civil servant, I think I'm not allowed to have an opinion on anything regarding him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The accused is asking a question. He's saying allegedly -- that allegedly there would have been an anti-Serb campaign launched and that Bernard Kouchner would have been the leader of that campaign. Have you heard about it? Is it true? Is it wrong?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Bernard Kouchner is known to be favourable to a kind of diplomacy that requires intervention from foreign states, from outside states, in order to help the people that are in the midst of a conflict. It is true that this is his leaning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What's more important to me is that you confirmed that you were a public servant and as such you cannot say anything about Bernard Kouchner. It's much more important than the opinion you stated. You as a public servant, you're also unable to be unbiased in this so-called expert report.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is different.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Otherwise you're a member of the board of directors of Le Courrier des Balkans. I'm sorry for my pronunciation.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was member of the board of directors, but I am no longer part of this board of directors for two years.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What matters to me is that you were. You also published a publication on the internet. And the president of that board of directors was Prince Njegos, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He lives in Paris as an emigre. This board of directors of yours was very committed and advocated fiercely the separation of Montenegro from Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Le Courrier des Balkans is a site that translates papers and articles from the papers in former Yugoslavia. It does not take position. It is not -- doesn't make any recommendations on foreign policy. Its main goal is to translate articles from the press in former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The way in which you selected articles was extremely tendentious and supported Montenegrin separatist inclinations?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not responsible for the editorial line. We have an editor-in-chief who is in charge of the editorial line. I was associated to this organisation or association as an outside researcher to see what kind of bridge could be set up between Le Courrier des Balkans and the academic world.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, regarding this question of Le Courrier des Balkans, you worked in this institution and within this institution. Is everybody perfectly neutral or do some people take sides or, as Mr. Seselj is saying, are there really editorial choices on Montenegro, for example?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Personally I translated a few articles either on request or articles that I selected myself, but my contribution was very small. I did not attend the regular meetings. The board of directors only met once or twice a year to run the internet site. But in daily activities I was not associated. This site appeared in the second half of the 1990s and its aim was to defend the independent media in the former republics of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, I have here a heap of your writings. First of all, reviewing your bibliography, I see you wrote very little academic works. You wrote mainly articles in the press genre, I would say. I have a large number of your texts. All of them are ideologically committed.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what you think. I mainly published articles in academic journals. I also wrote a few op eds for daily papers. But this is not my essential intellectual activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Which you call intellectual activity are political pamphlets, and in your texts, whenever you mention the Serbian Radical Party, you say that it's extreme or ultra-nationalist; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you use such adjectives it is in order to categorise. To identify parties, you have to qualify them depending on their programme, their ideology. My words, the words I used, were not at all inappropriate. It was not about casting a value judgement. It's not at all in the same way as the Socialist Party in Serbia who started a campaign in 1993 against radicals, saying that they were fascists, that they were primitive, and stressed crimes allegedly committed by volunteer units. That's not at all at the same level as I did. When I mentioned nationalism or ultra-right nationalist, I used categories as they're used in social sciences in order to identify political parties, to determine their identity. And even today with regard to the presidential elections, the recent elections in Serbia, all the press agencies spoke of Tomislav Nikolic as an ultra-nationalist. I myself was asked, interviewed by a Belgian radio some two weeks ago, and I criticised the use of such an adjective or noun because I thought that the candidate did not stress the national issue but mainly stressed economic and social issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: From what you just said it is evident that you operate with ideological categories rather than scientific and theoretical ones. You are engaged in day-to-day politics and you assume current ideological positions. There is no scientific apparatus in this. You want to see your text? They're all in French.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you take a certain text that are basically editorials, that cannot be compared to scientific papers published in academic journals which have a scientific character. You know, in daily newspapers you have op eds, editorials, and there are debates between people who may not be like-minded and when you write such texts you do not have any footnotes or any references to books, no bibliography. You can't put those texts on the same footing as academic papers published in academic journals where there is a committee selecting articles after careful, critical review.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, you only confirmed my belief that you are a daily press writer, not an academic, which we can see from your texts. You give answers that are too eloquent, wasting my precious time, as if you were coached by the Prosecution. What --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. He first has to answer. Yes, your objection, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What is the question? Mr. Seselj has made a series of statements. What is his question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Seselj, you must ask questions. The question that was contained but was not really properly expressed is this: The accused seems to say that you are a journalist rather than an academic, a scientific person. What is your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj stresses four or five texts which were editorials published in the media, and they are but a minute portion of what I may have published. You know, these are totally different ball games, as it were. I never really cast any value judgement as to the accused or his party.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Your works are full of value judgements. I asked you a question. What, in your opinion, does the word "extremist" mean, when I was interrupted by the Prosecutor. I'm sorry I didn't yet remember her name.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in France if you want to define political parties, some are said to be left wing, right wing, extreme droite, extreme gauche, far right, far left, and most interested in Serbia qualify the SRS as being from the extreme right. Why so? Because the party shows intolerance towards opinions that are not theirs, so the register, the tone, is in black and white, friend or enemy, friend or foe. If you're not a friend of their party, you are a traitor of the nation. And this is one of the reasons why the term is used. Now, as to extremists, parties that are called extremists may not necessarily resort to violence. Some may. Some may not.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, Mr. President, how much time has passed and I still haven't got an answer to my question, what the word "extremist" means or "extreme." This is a story for little children, what the witness is telling us. I want an answer to the question, what the word "extreme" means. And please take that into account. He is wasting at least 30 per cent of my time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This term is used: "Can you define the word extremist"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's not clearly defined by research either. It's in a position to moderates. There are political parties that have specific objectives and in order to implement them they use their means. Depending on the means and the objectives, the parties are qualified as moderate parties or less moderate. The latter are sometimes called extremist parties. But it is an expression, a term, used by most politologists, by historians. I did not invent it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my personal view, the answer that had been provided by the witness before, comparing extreme right and extreme left, lack intolerance, friend or foe, that was an answer given to the question about the definition of the term.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I note that this witness does not know what the term "extreme" means and he said himself that he didn't invent the term, and he is unable to explain it. What he has been telling is some sort of application of the term in political jargon. He is using a term, the meaning of which he doesn't know. But I'm moving on with my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What does the term "ultra" mean in the political sense? You said "ultra-nationalist," "ultra-nationalist person"? What does it mean politically?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say that I used it. I said that press agencies use the term, but I did not think it was adequate, for instance, with regard to the latest presidential election in Serbia. So this is ultra or hyper-nationalist, that puts the nation above all. It can have various meanings depending on the reality of a given country.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, in your text concerning the Serbian Radical Party you used the term "ultra-nationalist" and now suddenly you can't remember having used it. Are you going to say that you didn't use the term in your writings?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly, but if you have in mind certain texts, when were they published?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What I first want to know is whether you know the meaning of that term, "ultra." I see that you don't. Don't you ask me questions.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's certainly taken as an equivalent to "extreme" or "extremist."

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I am asking you what the term "ultra" means in the political sense. Just honestly say you don't know, if you don't know.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm trying to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you use the term "ultra-nationalist" in your report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't think so. I did not use the term, and as a rule in most of my work, I mean I'm known to be a serious researcher, I don't use that sort of terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you use the term "ultra" and "ultra-nationalist" in your less-serious or not-serious texts?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now you speak about certain texts, but maybe you should tell me what year you're interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'll tell you when I want to. Do you know what the term "radical" means?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, many definitions are possible. It can be a way of qualifying a policy defending principles in a strong way, in a vehement way, so defending that sort of principle, being very attached to them. There's also a radical political tradition.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So you don't know what the term "radical" means. Did you ever study Latin?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not study Latin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You wouldn't be able to tell us what the term "radics" means in Latin?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I didn't read Latin, I can't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very nice. Then you don't know what that term means and you are dealing with Greater Serbia and its ideological concept. When was the first time anybody presented the project of unification of all Serb lands? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there was a project of Serbs living at the end of the seventeenth century, those who lived in the Austrian Empire, but I can't remember the name. It didn't have a major impact after, later.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know who came forward with that project, the name of the man?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just told you that I didn't remember the name. He was a Serb in the Austrian Empire, and he had a political project going along the line of Greater Serbia; and it had been submitted to the authorities of the empire, so around 1697. I can't remember exactly. But this initiative did not leave a major imprint later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Don't make things up, Mr. Tomic. Do you know when was the last Turkish siege of Vienna?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1683.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'd object to the constant commentary on the witness' answers. Either he poses a question and he moves on, but to do that, I think, is inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Seselj, you do exactly what Mr. Milosevic used to do: You add commentaries to your questions. You must ask a question, he answers, and then you move on to another question and so on. If you want to make any comments, if you are clever, you put it into a question you want to put to the witness. For instance, now you said "You're inventing dates." He said "around 1697" so he doesn't know. He's not inventing.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's what I'm doing. I'm noting that the witness knows nothing, Mr. President. But he did know when the last Ottoman siege of Vienna and I congratulate him. But he doesn't know about Count Djordje Brankovic and his memo to the Austrian Emperor. And he's presenting his expert report in my trial. You don't know this, so we're moving on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When in history was the next time the term "Greater Serbia" was used? I see that you quoted in your bibliography the book of Mihailo Stanisic. That means you read the book. When was the next time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll take up the question. You were asked to write an expert report on the concept of the Greater Serbia. As a historian you should try to know who may have written on the topic and here you confess that you did not know that Count Djordje Brankovic - sorry if I misspell or mispronounce the name - that he had done some work on this topic at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The book just mentioned references made to this individual, but without any further detail, I don't know of any systematic study on this. As a rule, when this ideology is mentioned, one starts of the nineteenth century, as of the time when the national ideology is more clearly formulated. It may be that it had been expressed prior to that, but they're rarely taken into account in relation to the Greater Serbian project.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please go on, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And it's important to me for the Serbian public that all this be said here so that Serb historians could crack up laughing. Count Djordje Brankovic is the lighthouse of the entire Serbian concept.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: My question was not about the nineteenth century. That comes next. Who, in the beginning of the nineteenth century, mentioned the idea of Greater Serbia and the unification of Serbian lands?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait a minute. The Prosecutor is on her feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I again have an objection to the running commentary by Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This was again a commentary. Rather than do that, just take up the question again. You've just said that this concept was only studied in the nineteenth century, whilst there were others who studied this topic, for instance, Count Brankovic, and he can answer yes or no. That avoids the running commentary and also in this way the Prosecution will not object. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I repeated my question twice: Who was the first in the nineteenth century who mentioned that term and referred to the unification of all Serb lands? The question couldn't have been more direct.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, as of 1804, as the time of the first Serbian uprising, this idea is starting to take roots and together all the Serbs living around the Pasaluk, the Belgrade Pasaluk. Indeed, this idea may have been formulated by important people, leaders at the time, intellectuals. Later on the term was used by the Austrians. But now do we speak about Greater Serbia or the idea of unifying the Serbian people?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, thus you don't know that Arsenije Gagovic, the archbishop of Piva the monastery, in 1803, in Petrograd presented to the official representatives of the Russian government a plan about creating a Greater Serbia that would unify all Serb lands.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know it, but I didn't see any works on the Serbia mentioned at this initiative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So before answering, you understand the language of the accused and so you answer too quickly, too promptly, and the interpreters do not have time to interpret. So please wait a little before answering.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Shall I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Who is the next after Arsenije Gagovic who mentioned in writing the term "Greater Serbia" do you know? In writing.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not make a historical list of when the word "Greater Serbia" had been used. I looked at the -- what was done in the nineteenth century and this is in all books that deal with the history of the nineteenth century. I didn't go into details regarding all and looked into all possible projects that may have been devised. I just focused on the main projects. I did not write a detailed history of Serbia. I wrote a report, a hundred-page report. I wanted to be very clear and straightforward.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You, Mr. Tomic, do not know therefore that there were three very serious projects of Greater Serbia and the unification of Serb lands before Garasanin's Nacertanije, and you know that -- you don't know that the third project in 1804 was presented by the Serb metropolit Stevan Stratimirevic in his memorandum to the Russian emperor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not receiving interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please repeat because you were too fast in answering, and the interpreters couldn't follow. Mr. Seselj, please repeat your question you're too fast. You speak much too fast and the interpreters couldn't follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You have never heard that in 1804, the Serb metropolit Stevan Stratimirevic, in his memorandum to the Russian emperor presented a plan for creating a Greater Serbia by uniting all Serb lands, right?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well. When was the first time that a journal or a newspaper called "Greater Serbia" was started?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was at the end of 1880s.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know who started it?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not keep the name of this person in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It was started by an institution. What was the name of that institution?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Must have been a society or Drustvo Velika Srbija, probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The Greater Serbia Society, but you don't know that it was started by a great Serbian poet, Stevan Kacanski. Have you ever held this book in your hands?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher please take it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Would you read the title? We're only interested in the title, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The Print of All Issues of Greater Serbia - Journal from 1888 Until 1903."

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You've never held it in your hands?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that this journal existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What about this reprint? Have you ever held that?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not use it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know who, in 1903, started a second edition of Greater Serbia?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was one of the persons who was associated with this first publication, but I don't remember the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So you don't know that it was Dragutin Ilic, brother of a great Serbian poet Vojislav Ilic?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. These elements did not seem important to me. And when you talk about national Serbian ideas, you did not -- these journals are not mentioned. Of course you were interested when you published this magazine, Velika Srbija, to take a look at all -- everything that had been printed with this title since the beginning, but I'm not sure, I don't think that these publications were that important in the formulation of the national Serbian ideology.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Please don't waste my time with such explanations that have no importance whatsoever --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, objection. Of course the objection is sustained. Don't criticise, Mr. Seselj. Move onto something else. Don't criticise if you don't like the answer. I mean, you can ask questions that call for an answer of yes, no, I don't know. It's up to you to lead in a proper way and give the right questions in order to get the answers you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Tomic, when Greater Serbia was published as a daily?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During first -- during World War I.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Salonika.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Have you ever seen this book?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the reprint of this paper. I have it in my office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Biersay, do you want to see the book? Is that it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, to have them marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You'll be handed these books.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But before this I have a question for Mr. Seselj. Why is this journal -- why is the subtitle of this journal in Italian?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since you know absolutely everything about Greater Serbia, you must know why the subtitle is in Italian.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A counter-question. Is it also in French, "La Grande Serbie"? Is that also given in French, the subtitle?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's in Italian, and it means Serbia will be alone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because the idea of Greater Serbia follows the Italian great idea, "risorgimento," because the idea of Greater Serbia coincides with the idea of unification and liberation of Italy. Great men of the Italian national movement had a great influence on Serb intellectuals, Garibaldi and others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, since you were aware of the Salonika version of Greater Serbia, would you please have a look at one of the cover pages, any one of them. What is above the heading "Greater Serbia"?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Greater Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In French? It says "Le Grande Serbie" in French. Maybe my pronunciation is not great. Do you know why?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the Serb soldiers were fighting with the French soldiers around Thessaloniki in the eastern army with the French soldiers who were fighting in the eastern front.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Am I right when I say that the heading in French is there because we Serbs loved France at the time, almost as much as we loved Serbia itself?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a friendship that emerged between the two peoples during World War I, in as much that France welcomed a good number of Serbian refugees, notably children, and also because the two armies fought together from Saloniki in order to free territories that would later become part of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, do you know what -- where the other publications of the great Serbian newspaper? So we have this publication of Stevan Kacanski then we have this edition of Dragutin Ilic from 1903, then we have the Saloniki, one from 1916 to 1918. What others are there?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the war there may have been another series but I don't know it. I believe that these are documents that may be entitled "Greater Serbia" but they don't help us historians because there is no mention of the project of Serb unification in this, all these publications. I'm not the only one not to mention them. Most historians who worked on the Serbian ideology never mentioned these journals.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, I'm drawing the conclusion that with regard to something you haven't read, you assume you know in advance what it contains. You know about two pre-war series of the Greater Serbia, the Voljeva [phoen] and the Nis one?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You don't know that in the 20s in the Kingdom of Serbs and Slovenes, there was another two series between 1920 and 1926, one published by the Serbian party and another published by a group of intellectuals. You don't know that either, do you?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This party must have had a very marginal position. It was so marginal that it was never mentioned. I never saw it mentioned in the history of Yugoslavia between the two world wars. Serbia Stranka doesn't mean anything to me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you be so kind as to show this book as well to Mr. Tomic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'm wondering if we could mark for identification the now three books that Mr. Seselj is showing the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. If we give an MFI number -- well, that's one thing. We could always give an MFI number, but we need to know whether Mr. Seselj will eventually tender the entire book or only an excerpt of the book or the cover of the book or what exactly he wants to tender. Mr. Seselj, what's your purpose? If your purpose is to show that Greater Serbia is a notion that dates back to -- immemorial times, at least in the early nineteenth century as you are trying to prove in this journal, this collection of prints, where we see that there is a collection of several texts. I note that earlier there was a mention in Italian, and I know that in the second book it's in French, "Grande Serbie" in French. If this is your point, we can give an MFI number or a final number. If it's the entire content you're interested in, then we have a problem. The translation -- the CLSS will not translate this entire book. So, Mr. Seselj, what exactly is your point? These are exhibits coming from the Defence, so what do you want to do with them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I will be very precise. My ultimate goal is to fully discredit this expert report and these three large volumes are volumes I'm tendering as exhibits because of their visual impression, as an exhibit showing what this expert did not consult. So none of the texts in these books has to be translated. The size of the books is impressive as testimony to everything that the expert did not consult, as if you were to introduce into evidence a pistol or a knife that had been used to commit a crime. So they are not being tendered as documents but as objects. I hope you understand me. So there is no need to translate anything, but I want the books to be exhibited so that when the evidence is evaluated it can clearly be seen what this expert, who wrote an expert report, did not consult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. What's the position of the Prosecution? Mr. Seselj is saying that he has three books. He wants to create a visual impression and he is not asking for the content to be translated. He's not interested in the substance; he just wants to show that Greater Serbia was a concept that had been used, that had already been used by others, and that the expert witness did not consult at least these three books. Before answering I believe that the witness would like to say something. Mr. Tomic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. This term "Greater Serbia" may have been used, including by a French historian, Ernest Denis, who published a World War I book called "Greater Serbia." This could also be used by Vladimir Corovic, a Serbian historian who wrote a book in 1924 titled "Greater Serbia." Without these books being a research into the project of unification of the Serbian people. I looked at the book by Ernest Denis, and it described the historical and political life of Serbian nineteenth century, talking about the Yugoslav unification project rather than the Serbian unification project. Similarly, Djovic, in his book that was reprinted not as "Greater Serbia" but as "Unification," mentions the contribution of the Serbs to the Yugoslav unification process. So these are huge books and they do look big because these are a collection of journals, so these are reprints of papers. I have looked through the journal that was printed in Solaniki and I must say they are not necessarily essential to study Serbian nationalism.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. What about the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I think there are two issues, Your Honour. One is with respect to identifying the books just for the record. I'm not sure what the best way is to do that, whether it's through MFI or some other system, with the title, et cetera. The second thing is if we could have an opportunity to inspect these books, it's possible that even though Mr. Tomic did not consult these specific volumes, that he in fact did consult articles included in these volumes. So if we could just have an opportunity to review them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you want to review them, you'll have the whole night because you may have redirect, so you have the whole night. Mr. Mundis is helping you out and you have your language assistant. So I've answered one of your questions. We're going to give an MFI number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I must say that the MFI number as such, well, that's a provisional identification, a marking, to see whether the exhibit is going to be finally admitted as an exhibit. This is not to be ruled out. But look, this one is in B/C/S, so the Trial Chamber will never be able to review them. I would be opposed to this idea. I think that the transcript is enough for the purpose of the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Seselj, the Trial Chamber is of this view: If nobody plans to go to the substance of these three volumes and you just want to say, Look, there are three books, three collections of dailies published at the time or journals in which the topic of Greater Serbia can be found, that may be enough. Now, if the Prosecution wants to spend the whole night reviewing them, it's their own decision. Now, Mr. Seselj, is this it? You just want the Trial Chamber to be aware, to be made aware of the fact that there are collections of daily publications of the nineteenth century, late 1890s, that mention Greater Serbia? Is that all you wanted, Mr. Seselj? Let me add this: And you wanted to demonstrate that the witness did not know them or had not looked into them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, sir, I would like not to be interrupted by the witness. Mr. President, I think that the Prosecution has demonstrated so far incredible persistence in tendering the most irrelevant materials, including textbooks of military academies, command staff academies, and JNA war schools, 500 pages each, and all of it translated into English. Why am I insisting on having these books admitted into evidence, even if no one ever looks at them? I'm counting on the huge historical and legal significance of these trials and the future researchers who will look at the files. Not a single text has to be read. Nothing has to be translated. But this is impressive evidence that the witness did not know anything about this. That's what I insist on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. We're going to have numbers for the three books.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the three books will be marked MFI D10, D11, and D12, respectively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D10, D11, D12. Very well. So these books will be kept by the Registry. As you said, when we're gone, if there are ever researchers interested in what was said, they can look at them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to say that the Velika Srbija volume from 1916, I've got that one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is also in the transcript. It has been recorded. Please proceed, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The registrar is telling me that now we have to have a break. We're going to have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We're going to continue with the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, do you know when, after World War II, the periodical "Greater Serbia" came out?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first issue was published in July 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was there an illegal publication before that?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any prior issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So you're not aware that there was an illegal issue in the 1940s and early 1950s comprising 17 mimeographed issues.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you have in mind something that was published in the 1950s, after the Second World War and that was just circulated hand to hand because such publications could not be endorsed by the governing powers, no, I'm not aware of that document. Are they in the national library of Serbia today? I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: No, they are not in the national library of Serbia. There's an edition in the possession of the people who published it. One of them is Miodrag Jovicic, the late academician.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware. He's a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes, a member of the academy. But you don't know that he was one of the initiators of the illegal Xeroxed edition of "Greater Serbia" after World War II? You don't know that, did you?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know and I can explain you why. It was an underground publication so it was not in academic or university libraries not even in the national libraries, so it was very hard for me to consult that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But true scholarly researchers find ways of finding such things. But you're not a real scholarly researcher, are you?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only research into things I know and things that exist. And that was only circulated hand to hand. It was a kind of Samizdat. So these are publications that it's very hard to locate, to find at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know the name of the philosophical magazine, a periodical for philosophy, social sciences, and the social critique published by the Serbian Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there is a quarterly review or journal, I believe. Is it "Velika Srbija"? I can't remember the title exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: This means that you have never held that scholarly periodical in your hands.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it all depends on the date, the year, in which the first issue was published.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I can see from your response that you never held it in your hands. The first issue was published in the year 2000, and so far 70 volumes have been published.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's only normal that I focused on the documents that were published before the war broke out in the former Yugoslavia. I focused on statements and texts for the period from 1991 to 1995, and for the time beyond that, I thought this was outside my mission statement. As far as I could see it was only logical for me not to inspect this publication.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It's logical for you not to deal with a well-established scholarly periodical which published a large number of papers by renowned Serbian historian inter alia?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you be kind enough to hand Mr. Tomic an issue of this periodical.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: There are 70 volumes like this one that have been published, Mr. Tomic. Please be kind enough to read out loud the name of the periodical.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Serbian Free Thought."

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That's volume 13, is it not?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough to turn to page 25, please. It can be put on the ELMO, too. What do you see on page 25, Mr. Tomic?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the book written by Denis called "The Greater Serbia."

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough to turn to page 161. You have a part of the text here which has been marked. Would you be kind enough to read it, as you speak Serbian and read Serbian? Just what has been marked, the last paragraph and then it continues on the next page for a bit.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The pan-Serbian programme is not the product of the imagination of a handful of dreamers. History and ethnography have imposed it on politicians."

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Go on.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm waiting for the interpreters. "It follows from the consciousness of the people who, for several centuries, have aspired by continual and unanimous effort to join together the fate of its members. It follows from this clearly without violating the principles of international justice and without impinging upon the deepest and most natural feelings of the southern people."

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Turn to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Bosnia-Herzegovina and the tri-unitary Kingdom of Croatia, Slavonia and Dalmatia must without doubt be the part of the new Serbian kingdom."

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know when the book by Ernest Denis was first published in Serbian?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, but it was published in French in 1915, during the First World War.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: No wonder you don't know because never before was it published in Serbian. This is its first edition in the Serbian language. Mr. Tomic, have you read the whole of Ernest Denis's book or have you just leafed through it or have you just found its title in a bibliography?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have read it. Maybe you have to check the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is it clear to you, Mr. Tomic, as you have read the book, that Ernest Denis included in the territory of Greater Serbia all the southern Slav territories with the exception of a Bulgaria, all the territories inhabited by Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He, first and foremost, speaks to the Yugoslav unification project and he does indeed include all those territories into the project defended by the government, the Soviet government at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question for you. I did not know who Ernest Denis was. I discovered this during the examination-in-chief led by Milosevic together with Seselj when he was a witness and this name appeared as part of the questions. You knew that you were to testify. You didn't look into his work, knowing that he might -- had written about Greater Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was a Sabon professor specialised in the Czech and Slovak worlds, and he was supposed to have been paid by the Soviet government at the time in order to champion the interests of Serbia to France.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How do you know this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I forgot the exact source, but at the time it was common practice in the "Journal Illustre des Temps." It was frequent for journalists to be paid by outside governments in order for their opinions to be promoted to the French public opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it different today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that things have evolved and developed since then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So you are now trying to discredit the renowned Professor Ernest Denis and his good intentions. You say that he was paid by the Serbian government but you don't know the source of this information. Can a true scholar present things in this way?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course this should be verified, but this is something that I saw in books that I had in my hands. But this being said, this book mainly mentions the Yugoslav unification project. It may have beared the title of "Greater Serbia" but it is not a book in which the project of unifying Serbs is stated and set out clearly or in a systematic way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, you evidently haven't read the book because had you read it you would have seen that Ernest Denis considers that all Croats are in fact Serbs; is that correct? But as you haven't read the book, you don't know that. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He certainly mentions close peoples, mentioning Serbs and Croats, and among the political and intellectual elites of the time there was a view that Serbs and Croats were one and the same nation. It was a common thing at the time in educated circles.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But he sees the unification of Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes in the Kingdom of Greater Serbia. Isn't that what he says explicitly in his book?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the title says "Greater Serbia" but in fact at the time that was the name given to Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: At that time, Mr. Tomic, there was no Yugoslavia in existence. It should be clear to you that the first common state was called the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was, indeed, the official name.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tomic, in your expert report you include the false information that Professor Ernest Denis was being paid by the Serbian government to write such a book and now you say that you don't know from what source you got this information; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I found this information in Velika Srbija, Stanisic's book that deals with Greater Serbian projects.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now you think --

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stanisic, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You were able to read in Stanisic's book on all the predecessors of Vuk Karadzic as regards the ideology of Greater Serbia, but we see that you don't remember it. And now you are not sure you found it in Stanisic. You don't know where you found it, and yet you include it in your expert report. And there's no footnote giving us your source. So you have included a serious unverified accusation against the renowned Professor Denis; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I read history and in classes and courses this phenomena was mentioned, for instance, regarding this daily called Le Temps, some Slav studying professors had been paid to defend the causes -- professors had been paid to defend the causes of Serb people. So when I read this piece of information, it did not seem to be unfounded. Because this work is mentioned but another one as well of the same tenet.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And where is your foundation? You have very suspect thesis because you're no kind of intellectual or scholar. Isn't that right, Mr. Tomic?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You should have put the question in a better way. You should have asked this: Are you an intellectual? You can answer yes, no. Are you a scientist? You can answer yes or no. So what do you say? Because Mr. Seselj is challenging you, so what do you have to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My position, my job, is regarded as an intellectual job, and I also conducted research that was validated by university, academic institutions, scientific work. Now, maybe I should have been more curious maybe in this particular respect and checked this point further, but in my view this work on Greater Serbia was not essential. I was mainly interested in knowing how intellectuals or Serbian political leaders formulated the ideology themselves, and I was not so much interested in finding out other external academics, such as French academics, might have thought of the question, people that were not from there. Indeed, this book is not essential.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, Mr. President, let me remind you that I do have the right to put leading questions during cross-examination. Therefore, my question was proper. I made a statement and asked if it was correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Secondly, Mr. Tomic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are right but that's not the problem. The problem is that Ms. Dahl made an objection. She was saying that you are proceeding with a different confirmations and statements and you're supposed to ask questions. And I'm sorry, it's not Ms. Dahl, I always have Ms. Dahl in mind. It's Ms. Biersay. I was an entire year with her, and her name is in my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I have already forgotten about Ms. Dahl.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, you say that you were not primarily interested in what foreigners wrote about the project of Greater Serbia, but you stated what Ernest Denis wrote in your expert report and you put in the unfounded claim that he was a mercenary of the Serbian government, that he was on their payroll. In every Serbian university such a scholar would be thrown out immediately. How is that possible? If you have nothing to say in reply, I am moving on to my next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, he did not directly assess Professor Ernest Denis. He just repeated what he had seen that had been written on this person and on other French academics at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But, Madam Judge, that's precisely the problem, that he doesn't say who wrote -- that Ernest Denis was on the payroll of the Serbian government. Maybe a French intellectual was indeed on the payroll of the Serbian government. I don't know. I never dealt with this. I know that Ernest Denis was not. Ernest Denis is a great name, a luminary, especially for the history of Slav peoples, not only Serbs. And here a great scholar is slandered without a shred of evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So, Mr. Tomic, let's move on. Please turn to page 173, if the usher would be so kind as to put it on the ELMO. Page 173 of this magazine of the Serbian Radical Party. This book by Milan Jevtic is something you have never seen; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That book is in the Serbian language and was published in New York in 19 -- it's a book that was published in Serbian, I was saying, in New York in 1919. Since you have never seen it before I am not going to dwell on it. I cannot examine you on a book you haven't read, right? Could you please turn to page 287. That is the front page of the book by Vladimir Corovic, "Greater Serbia," that you were aware of, published in 1924.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Have you read that book?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Based on the reading of that book, was it clear to you that Vladimir Corovic believed that Greater Serbia had been realised by the relation of the Kingdom of Croats, Serbs, and Slovenes. Isn't that the main thought of this book?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this book Vladimir Corovic systematically presented the Serbian unification project, and Rados Lucic, who is a well-known historian in Serbia, in the -- something written in this book in the post phase as well as something written on Serbia, this person says that when he wrote "Velika Srbija," this book "Velika Srbija," he was not thinking of the Serbian unification project but the Yugoslav unification project. As I said earlier the reprint of this book was no longer "Velika Srbija" because it seemed that it created a problem but [French spoken]. So the author changed the title in order to have a title that would really correspond to the substance of the book, because in this book "Velika Srbija" the point was not to define the Serbian unification project.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please, there's something I don't understand. You keep repeating this word "Yugoslav," but for a period where Yugoslavia did not exist. Do you mean southern Slavs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, the term had already been coined in early -- early in the second part of the nineteenth century. The Yugoslav project was already existing and there were people who defined themselves as such, Yugoslavs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But in other languages, like in French, because the French was very interested in all this, so were they talking about Yugoslavia or were they talking about a territory that would bring together all Slavs from the south, or southern Slavs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that we were talking not of Yugoslavia but Yugoslavs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First, so everybody can understand, can you make a difference between Greater Serbia and this concept of Yugoslavs? Is there a difference? If so, please tell us where.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in Ernest Denis's book he's mixing Greater Serbia and the Yugoslav unification project. When he's talking about Greater Serbia, when he's talking about this the process by which southern Slavs can be unified, minus the Bulgarians. At the time the main idea was the Croats and the Serbs were the one and only nation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They are Slavs from the south.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Slavs from the south. And in the elite circles and -- the idea was that Serbs and Croats and also the Slovenes were part and parcel of what -- one unique nation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if I understand, this concept of Yugoslavs deals with Slavs from the south.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Slavs from the south. But this project of unification did not include the Bulgarians. They are also Slavs from the south but they were not included. So it was mainly Slovenes, Croats, and Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because -- I'm asking you the etymology of it. "Yugoslav" means Slavs of the south. "Yugo" is "south."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just have to note one thing to avoid misunderstanding among the Judges. We see precisely from this that Croats are considered to be Serbs of Catholic faith because they speak Serbian, and that's why the concept of Greater Serbia encompasses all Croats because there are very few Croats who did not speak original Serbian, who speak the Cakavian dialect, or the Cakavian dialect. But the witness doesn't understand this. I just want to show you that this witness has not read the book of Vladimir Corovic. Look at the last passage in the book that I marked. Could you put it on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "All the great things that we have today achieved by superhuman effort remains as a legacy to the younger generations for them to develop it and make it more complete. Raising above us, they should naturally rise higher than we did. We can with a clear conscience say that few generations left to their heirs more than we are leaving to ours. To estimate the contribution of individuals or individual regions to this is difficult. But one thing is doubtless: The role of Serbia in this sense was the hardest and the greatest, the noblest. If a man is allowed to express wishes for the future, then we have only one."

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: "In the souls of the new generation there should always be an understanding --"

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a quote, you know, from a book that is more than a hundred pages long and I'm talking about the substance of the book, so we don't have the same approach at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But I am pointing to the conclusion, the last passage, the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The transcript does not contain all of this, including one question and one answer that we missed because it's going too fast.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I wish to tender this entire issue of the magazine. Of course it contains relevant passages, but the magazine itself, this issue, is evidence to all the witness does not know and what matters has been read into the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could we have a number for this book?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be MFI D13.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You spoke in the examination-in-chief at length about the London Agreement and then you spoke about certain repercussions that the London Agreement should have had in Serbia after the First World War, and here in your own hand, you drew what the map of Serbia should have looked like according to the London Agreement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Put it on the ELMO, please, to remind the Trial Chamber and the new very likeable representative of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That's what drew yourself, isn't it, Mr. Tomic?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that it was quite a crude line, rough line, because I did it very quickly. But it corresponds to the [indiscernible] that was next to Cape Blanca, under Cape Blanca, to the border with Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'm interested in this northern border. It is approximately along the Sava River, isn't it? Isn't it?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mean, I did not have any geographical landmarks so this is really a rough line. You can't regard this as something done by a geographer or cartographer. I had no space at all. I was not sitting properly. I mean that was the idea I wanted to convey, that basically de facto, since part of the littoral of the Adriatic Sea was given to Serbia, the forces of the Entente tried to give Bosnia and Herzegovina to Serbia. And I tried to illustrate this. I'm not claiming that these borders, including the northern one, would be accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Tomic. I wouldn't have been able to draw this precisely myself. But we agree that only after the conclusion of the London Agreement were there additional negotiations between the Kingdom of Serbia and western powers. Do we agree on that point? And these negotiations took place from time to time on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were negotiations between the countries of the Entente as to the territorial compensations to be given to Serbia because Banija had to be given to Romania and a good part of Macedonia to Bulgaria. So during the summer in July and August, more specifically in 1915, there were exchanges between the various foreign ministries of the Entente countries and the territories given to Serbia during that summer were extended indeed to Slavonia and the Srem region.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, you did not encompass Slavonia in this map?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's only normal because I was speaking about the Treaty of London signed on the 26th of April, so I drew those nine as of a specific date, 26th of April, 1915.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, with the Treaty of London itself, Bosnia-Herzegovina was not an issue.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, this was a consequence of the treaty. How could part of the coastline be given to Serbia if the hinterland is not Serbian? It's one of the consequences of the treaty. Already at the time, Bulgaria had made territorial claims in Macedonia against the interests of Serbia. As early as the autumn of 1914 there was this will to give Bosnia-Herzegovina as a kind of compensation. That was the consequence of the Bulgarian claims regarding Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, you keep avoiding an answer. Why? The Treaty of London was trying to resolve the issue of Italian ambitions on the Adriatic coast. Serbia had a marginal role. Only after the conclusion of the Treaty of London, allies negotiate with the Serbian government territorial compensations to Serbia. Is that correct? Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I wrote clearly in my report. I did write that the Treaty of London defined how the coastline was divided into several countries and did not deal with the issues of the territories on hinterland. Only in the ensuing months in July and August, for instance, only then were the new proposal -- and these are territorial compensations, but Serbia itself was not involved in the negotiations. It may have known of them, but it was not taking part directly in the negotiations since Russia, France, UK, the Entente countries, and Italy in part were involved in negotiations. At the time Italy --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's shed some light on this. If I understood properly, the purpose of the Treaty of London was to give Italy parts of territory on the Adriatic coastline. We see a map here which is very telling in this respect, because in the shaded parts we can see Italian demands of 4th of March, 1915, so we have the impression that actually Italy is in the driving seat, that it was to reclaim some territory. So that's -- Bosnia and Herzegovina, there, you said that will come later or that came later as part of some compensation; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As early as the autumn of 1914 the Entente countries tried to push Bulgaria to start war against the central powers, but the Bulgarians had some claims on Macedonia, and it was then envisaged to give some territorial compensation. Part of Macedonia would be taken from Serbia. It was regarded as an important territory for Serbia. One thought that it would be fair to compensate that by giving Bosnia-Herzegovina to Serbia. But that's not the essential part in the treaty. The treaty basically defines the boundaries. But these are two parallel developments. On the one hand, the coastline is being divided and defined, but parallel to this you have the issue of territorial compensations given to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My intellectual curiosity is aroused. I see a shaded area in the south of Valena. Why did Italy want to have this small piece of land?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To have and control the access to the Adriatic Sea. It was a strategic part. They did everything they could to set up Italian soldiers there. Also by initiating trouble in that area in order to justify the Italian's intervention. But that is the access to the Adriatic Sea, and they wanted to occupy this piece of land at all cost.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please go on, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, you keep confusing things, confusing events from 1915 and the involvement of Bulgaria in the war with the repercussions of the Treaty of London on the attitude of the powers of the Entente of Serbia towards 1916. It's true that the allies wanted to take away territories of Serbia and give them to Bulgaria in order to involve Bulgaria in the war on the side of the Entente, but Bulgaria eventually did join the war on the side of the central powers. That issue was resolved. In 1916 the Entente negotiates with Serbia about territorial compensations because of huge suffering from the war and great casualties of Serbia. I have a book here by an important Croatian author, a very renowned one. Could you please show the front page of this book.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Mr. Seselj is speaking too fast.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Italy, Allies, and the Yugoslav Issue."

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you see the name of the author?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dragovan Jepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: A renowned Croatian historian. Do you see where the book was published?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Zagreb in 1970.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Please be so kind as to put the map on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The speakers overlap all the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Both for the witness and for Mr. Seselj, we are told by the interpreters that you're overlapping and both of you are speaking too fast. Please respect once again the pause and not to speak too fast. Remember, there are persons trying to interpret what you are saying.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try, Judge. Could you show on the ELMO, please, this map. I don't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What is written in the key?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Just a point of clarification, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Excuse me. A point of clarification. What is the provenance of this map that Mr. Seselj is showing the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
