utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. What is the provenance? Does it come from Stjepic's book? Where does it come from?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The map is from Stjepic's book. You see even the logo of the book. I didn't bring the whole book. One cannot fax such a large one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Look at the title of the key. Could you please read it out.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Territorial Promises of the Powers of the Entente to Serbia, 16 August 1915."

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you see that there is no mention of any compensation to Bulgaria anymore? Is that clear from this map?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you see that it was envisaged to give half of Dalmatia to Serbia, the entire coastline of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was indeed the intention of the Entente countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you see that northern Albania was also planned to become part of Serbia, together with the Skadar lake?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, during the war there was this idea of splitting of Banija into too, and part of it to Greece, the other to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And Italy.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the small area around Verona to Italy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you see here that the entire Slavonia and Srem were supposed to become part of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are territories promised to Serbia in 1915, so we're not talking about the Treaty of London. That was if Banat was given to Romania and Serbia wanted Banat to be part of the future state of the southern Slavs because they thought that it was an area just adjacent to Belgrade, and Belgrade had to be made secure. So the capital needed some hinterland, they thought. You can see that if Banat goes to Romania, the Romanian border is basically on the doorstep of Belgrade. So by way of compensation, the Entente countries gave Slavonia, Srem, and the Dutch region. That has nothing to do with the London Treaty because I was talking about the one of the 26th of April, 1915, and here we're talking about later negotiations held during the summer of that year. So indeed this map matches the will of the Entente countries as expressed in August 1915. And I must note that in many books this map is presented as being the map of the Treaty of London of 1915. So there is confusion, including in Serbia, because they mix them up. And it's true that in a matter of weeks the Serbian borders changed. It changed from day to day. I myself looked in archives in the Quai d'Orsay in the foreign ministry premises on the Treaty of London. I reviewed dispatches by Delcasi [phoen], the foreign minister, to all the ambassadors concerned. The answers from the Great Britain, Russia and Italy. So indeed this map corresponds to the will of the Entente countries as expressed in August 1915 and not on the 26th of April, 1915, which is the date the Treaty of London was signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, you quite arbitrarily put Bosnia-Herzegovina into the text of the Treaty of London. The Treaty of London deals exclusively with the territorial ambitions of Italy and the Serbian coast on the Adriatic Sea. All the rest are repercussions of the Treaty of London in further negotiations. You don't understand the Treaty of London as a beginning of a process, do you?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is to be seen as part of a process that started in autumn 1914 redefining the Balkan space, essentially. And it's hard to imagine that if part of the coastline were given to Serbia, it's hard to imagine that the hinterland, therefore, Bosnia and Herzegovina, would not be part of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, so that map of yours was a product of your imagination because it was difficult for you to imagine it differently. Did I understand this correctly?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not my map anyway. This comes from work done on Italy and only was concerned with the Treaty of London as such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During examination-in-chief, we also dwelled on this aspect of the issue and you clarified that this was only a consequence, as the witness saw it, of the Treaty of London. That's how I understood things.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But, Madam Judge, I'm trying to prove that the witness is an ignoramus. The consequence is the entire Slavonia, not that border on the Sava. That map he drew in his own hand, I guarantee to you that he had never seen it. Such a map doesn't exist anywhere. The only map that exists is this one. I'm trying to show you that the witness is an ignoramus. That's the point, if you allow this intervention.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're talking about two different moments in time. I have looked at the diplomatic cables at the time and borders were changing all the time. At one point in time people were even wondering whether Croatia should be handed over to Serbia. Italy was against that very strongly. So there are negotiations dealing with -- giving satisfaction to the Italians what they wanted on the Dalmatian coast, and that ended up with the Treaty of London; and then we have on the other hand also negotiations that dealt with the compensations to be given to Serbia. So this map that we have here on the screen corresponds to this later negotiations dealing with the territorial compensations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if I understand, because we've seen several maps, one of which you drew yourself, but the one we have here on your screen which comes from Mr. Stjepic's book, this is the outcome of negotiations that were held after the Treaty of London, since it was August 16, 1915.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this comes after the Treaty of London.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, after the Treaty of London and after a great number of negotiations on the Entente countries regarding what kind of territorial compensations should be given to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the first map we saw with the Dalmatian coast and so on, that was the map that dealt exactly with the Treaty of London, April 16, 1915, at that moment in time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But when you, in your own hand, drew the border, was that for April or was that for August?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it was a consequence of the Treaty of London.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it was April.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time was part of the Austro-Hungarian Empire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So when you drew that border, in your mind you were thinking, Treaty of London, April 1915.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, everything is very clear now. I hope everything is clear for Mr. Seselj. If not, I'm sure he will continue asking questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, everything has been clear to me for a long time. I'm trying to show to you that the expert drew the border ad hoc. The Treaty of London is a fundamental agreement and it was developed over the following few years. The map that the witness created didn't exist anywhere. He drew it arbitrarily, and he said something else here. He said that from this map here one can see that Banat is divided between Serbia and Romania, but this is not true. All of Banat here is envisaged as belonging to Romania. It was only later that Serbia got part of Banat. You can see that Banat was supposed to be part of Romania and yet the witness said that the division of Banat between Serbia and Romania had been agreed on. You can see that he knows nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I understand the problem now. When you're drawing the map yourself and when you're drawing the border yourself, at that point in time you are not drawing the borders of the Treaty of London.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we had a discussion on the Treaty of London and we were talking about the consequences of such treaty. So since part of the coastline was given to Serbia, then in the minds of the countries of the Entente, Bosnia-Herzegovina had to be given to Serbia and this is why I drew the map, to illustrate these consequences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but you say that this was in the mind of the negotiators. But in April 1915, when the treat was actually signed between all parties, this hadn't been planned yet, this hadn't been envisaged, at least on paper?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the map drawn illustrates the consequences of the treaty. I don't think it's an official map that was drawn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but with our indictment, you know, and the problem of Greater Serbia, that's the crux of the problem. When I see this map drawn in August 1915, the powers, you know, that are involved in the Treaty of London agree, they will give Bosnia, Herzegovina and Slavonia to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. And everybody agrees. Italy, France, and the two other ones involved.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Italy is very cautious, much more than the others. France was ready to hand over Croatia to Serbia during the summer of 1915, but Italy was against it because it believed that this territory had to be kept as a bait for the Austrians in order to bring the Austrians in war against the Hungarians.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Hungarians against Austria.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was the ministry of foreign affairs had in mind at the time. But the Serbian government at the time had a much broader objective. What they wanted was the unification of Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes, and so the borders that you have that were envisaged here by the Entente countries did not correspond to what the Serbian government at the time had in mind because what they had in mind would have much more greater territorial consequences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Seselj, you have ten minutes left before we adjourn.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, you see that I agree with the Entente because the western border here is almost identical to mine. That's what I wanted to show. But as we have little time left, I only wish to draw attention -- the witness' attention, who said that in his text he did not use expressions such as "extreme Serbian Radical Party," "the extreme right of Vojislav Seselj," "ultra-rightest," and so on. I want to remind him --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. Before we move to this topic, we must give a number to these two documents, for the map and for the book title.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the map will be marked for identification as D14, and the title of the book, D15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please resume.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to remind the witness that on the 5th of October, 2000, in the magazine "Le Courrier des Balkans," I may have mispronounced it because I do not speak French. He published a text: "Serbia Finally a Democratic Revolution."

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is that right, Mr. Tomic? Do you remember that text of yours?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe I'm not the one who came up with the title.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, it doesn't matter. Somebody else may have given it its title. Do you remember the text in?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In a sentence in the fifth paragraph you wrote: "The political scene has really been cleaned up. The Serbian Radical Party, an ultra-rightest formation of Vojislav Seselj, has been almost destroyed."

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I used these terms. I would like to have the text in French to compare. It's very hard to discuss a text if I don't have the original version under my eyes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe Mr. Seselj has the document and we will put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here it is in French. I have it all, Judge. Only what has been marked for now. You also have it in French.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have the entire text. I will only give my opinion when I have the full text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Seselj, this is only an excerpt.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if he doesn't remember, let him give me back this piece of paper. I can't carry all the texts around with me in French. I have a vast quantity of texts, but I don't speak French so it's hard for me to find my way about the text. If I had an assistant, I might be able to do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you write in a quote: "The political scene has been cleaned? The Serbian Radical Party, ultra-nationalist Serbian formation was swamped." Did you write that? If this is in quotes, it's probably because it was a passage that was quoted from your article. You don't remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember. I can only give you my opinion if I have the entire text. This is something I wrote in 2000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, please ask a question. The witness has reservations about the content, but maybe you have a question to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, let's go to example number 1. That was example number 3. Let's look at example number 1. Do you remember this text of yours?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the yearly situation in "Etude du Monde" in 1998 where I take stalk of what happened in the country economically and politically. And I qualify the Serbian Radical Party as far right, extreme far right, but I'm not the only one to do this. This is an expression that is used to characterise a party in order for the French people to know exactly what we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. Tomic, but a little while ago you were unable to explain what the expression "extreme" means. That's what the problem is. Look at example number 2.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Let's look at example number 4.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The far right" in France, the Serbian Radical Party, for researchers and for social scientists as well as for reporters, is a party that is on the far right of the political spectrum.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But one can assume that other researchers know what the expression "extreme" means and you don't know. Look at example number 4. Would you look at that, please. Is this from a text of yours?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, here I remember this better. I put this under -- in quotes because there was supposedly a democratic side and a nationalist side, the nationalist side being extremist and authoritarian. But this is not a judgement of value. This is a characterisation of the two political sides that were head on in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you're saying "confronted with the extremist danger of the SRS," what do you mean exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm talking about the possibility of the Serbian Radical Party winning the elections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And why would that be a danger? A danger for democracy? If we read the sentence that's above, I would see that is-- what you mean, the democrats on the one side and the others.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there's a danger. For the Serbian Radical Party, the Greater Serbia is still something that's topical and that's the problem -- and that's crux of the problem again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I think we have to call it a day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Look at number 6. Please let's just deal with this because this would round off this set of questions. Just example 6. Could you just look at example 6. Is this from a text of yours?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't seem to identify this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In French you're saying: "The result, the outcome, of this is a very strong frustration which is reflected by the ultra-nationalist vote for Vojislav Seselj's SRS." So what did you mean there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't even identify this text. These are -- Recontre de Balkans, national identities in the Balkans. This is probably some colloquialism that was held up and a summary must have been made. But I don't know if this was something I wrote myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. He doesn't know. Please finish with your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tomic participated in this discussion and his participation can be found on the internet. The entire discussion can be seen on the internet. My investigators found it there. If he doesn't remember it, then give me back my examples and we're finished with that. I only put this forward to show to you that he uses the expressions "ultra" and "extremist" without knowing their meaning. He was unable to explain what these terms mean. That's the crux of the matter. If he doesn't remember this, all the better for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now, for tomorrow, Mr. Seselj, let me tell you that you've already spent 1 hour and 35 minutes. You had 4 hours, so you've already used 1 hour and 35 minutes so you can compute what's left for you. I'll come back to one question because the legal officer reminded me of one thing. When your associates will come, they are coming as civilians. They won't be wearing a robe, right? They don't have a black robe; they're in plain clothes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. They will speak in their own name but they cannot take the floor, they cannot ask questions. You're the only one to ask questions and to lead the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If necessary they will pass a piece of paper to me or help me with a document. Only in that case would they be active; otherwise they will not participate. And of course they will introduce themselves to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Everything is crystal clear. Witness, you will be back in this courtroom tomorrow at 2.15 because we're sitting in the afternoon. So we'll all meet tomorrow at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may say, the Trial Chamber can have all my publications. My newspapers -- my reviews, my articles, everything that I have ever written, the Trial Chamber can have it, if it needs it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
